claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Candida albicans last shared a common ancestor approximately 300 million years ago.
source: In the human pathogen Candida albicans (which last shared a common ancestor with S. cerevisiae some 300 million years ago), we show that different regulators, Rtg1 and Rtg3, activate the three GAL genes.
evidence: The manuscript cites this timeframe as established knowledge about the divergence of these species.

claim: In Candida albicans, Rtg1 and Rtg3 activate the three GAL genes.
source: In the human pathogen Candida albicans (which last shared a common ancestor with S. cerevisiae some 300 million years ago), we show that different regulators, Rtg1 and Rtg3, activate the three GAL genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the transcriptional regulator Gal4 binds and activates the GAL genes.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the transcriptional regulator Gal4 binds and activates these genes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about S. cerevisiae GAL gene regulation.

claim: The overall logic of GAL gene regulation is the same in both S. cerevisiae and C. albicans—the GAL genes are induced by galactose.
source: Using single-cell dynamics and RNA-sequencing, we demonstrate that although the overall logic of regulation is the same in both species—the GAL genes are induced by galactose—there are major differences in both the quantitative response of these genes to galactose and in the position of these genes in the overall transcription network structure of the two species.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell dynamics and RNA-sequencing experiments.

claim: There are major differences in the quantitative response of GAL genes to galactose between S. cerevisiae and C. albicans.
source: Using single-cell dynamics and RNA-sequencing, we demonstrate that although the overall logic of regulation is the same in both species—the GAL genes are induced by galactose—there are major differences in both the quantitative response of these genes to galactose and in the position of these genes in the overall transcription network structure of the two species.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell dynamics and RNA-sequencing experiments.

claim: There are major differences in the position of GAL genes in the overall transcription network structure between S. cerevisiae and C. albicans.
source: Using single-cell dynamics and RNA-sequencing, we demonstrate that although the overall logic of regulation is the same in both species—the GAL genes are induced by galactose—there are major differences in both the quantitative response of these genes to galactose and in the position of these genes in the overall transcription network structure of the two species.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell dynamics and RNA-sequencing experiments.

claim: The three Leloir enzymes (a kinase, epimerase and transferase) are conserved across all kingdoms of life.
source: Here we describe an evolutionary analysis of a transcriptional circuit controlling the production of enzymes that convert galactose to glucose-1-phosphate via the Leloir pathway (Kew and Douglas, 1976); these enzymes (a kinase, epimerase and transferase) are conserved across all kingdoms of life (Holden et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Holden et al., 2003.

claim: In most organisms, expression of the three Leloir enzymes increases when galactose is present in the growth medium.
source: In most organisms, expression of the three Leloir enzymes increases when galactose is present in the growth medium (Holden et al., 2004); this regulation has been extensively studied in the budding yeast S. cerevisiae (Campbell et al., 2008; Conrad et al., 2014; Giniger et al., 1985; Johnston, 1987; Lohr et al., 1995; Ptashne and Gann, 2003; Sellick and Reece, 2006; Traven et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holden et al., 2004 and multiple other references.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, Gal4 binds to short sequence motifs in the upstream region of GAL1, GAL7 and GAL10 genes and induces their transcription when galactose is present and glucose is absent.
source: Here the zinc cluster transcriptional regulator Gal4 binds to short sequence motifs in the upstream region of the genes encoding these enzymes (GAL1, GAL7 and GAL10) and induces their transcription when galactose is present and glucose is absent.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about S. cerevisiae GAL gene regulation.

claim: The expression of GAL1 in S. cerevisiae has been estimated to be <1 mRNA molecules/10 cells in glucose and ~35 mRNA molecules/cell in galactose.
source: The expression of GAL1 has been estimated to be <1 mRNA molecules/10 cells in glucose and ~35 mRNA molecules/cell in galactose (Iyer and Struhl, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Iyer and Struhl, 1996.

claim: The induction ratio of GAL1 in S. cerevisiae is greater than 350 fold.
source: Due in part to this high induction ratio (>350 fold), Gal4 has been adapted as a tool to artificially turn genes on and off in many animal and plant species (Brand and Perrimon, 1993; Fischer et al., 1988; Hartley et al., 2002; Kakidani and Ptashne, 1988; Waki et al., 2013; Webster et al., 1988).
evidence: This is calculated from the expression levels cited from Iyer and Struhl, 1996.

claim: Gal4 has been adapted as a tool to artificially turn genes on and off in many animal and plant species.
source: Due in part to this high induction ratio (>350 fold), Gal4 has been adapted as a tool to artificially turn genes on and off in many animal and plant species (Brand and Perrimon, 1993; Fischer et al., 1988; Hartley et al., 2002; Kakidani and Ptashne, 1988; Waki et al., 2013; Webster et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The C. albicans genome contains an unmistakable ortholog of each Leloir pathway enzyme.
source: The Candida albicans genome contains an unmistakable ortholog of each Leloir pathway enzyme (Brown et al., 2009; Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Martchenko et al., 2007a), arranged in a cluster as they are in S. cerevisiae (Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Slot and Rokas, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2009; Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Martchenko et al., 2007a.

claim: The Leloir pathway enzymes in C. albicans are arranged in a cluster as they are in S. cerevisiae.
source: The Candida albicans genome contains an unmistakable ortholog of each Leloir pathway enzyme (Brown et al., 2009; Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Martchenko et al., 2007a), arranged in a cluster as they are in S. cerevisiae (Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Slot and Rokas, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Slot and Rokas, 2010.

claim: C. albicans contains a clear ortholog of the transcriptional regulator Gal4.
source: It also contains a clear ortholog of the transcriptional regulator Gal4 (Martchenko et al., 2007b; Sellam et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Martchenko et al., 2007b; Sellam et al., 2010.

claim: In C. albicans, Gal4 does not play a role in expressing the three GAL enzymes.
source: However, in C. albicans, which last shared a common ancestor with S. cerevisiae at least 300 million years ago (Taylor and Berbee, 2006), Gal4 does not play a role in expressing the three GAL enzymes (Martchenko et al., 2007a); instead, it has been implicated as having a subsidiary role in regulating glucose utilization (Askew et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Martchenko et al., 2007a.

claim: In C. albicans, Gal4 has been implicated as having a subsidiary role in regulating glucose utilization.
source: However, in C. albicans, which last shared a common ancestor with S. cerevisiae at least 300 million years ago (Taylor and Berbee, 2006), Gal4 does not play a role in expressing the three GAL enzymes (Martchenko et al., 2007a); instead, it has been implicated as having a subsidiary role in regulating glucose utilization (Askew et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Askew et al., 2009.

claim: Despite being uncoupled from Gal4, the three GAL genes in C. albicans are transcriptionally activated when galactose is present and glucose is absent in the growth medium.
source: Despite being uncoupled from Gal4, the three GAL genes in C. albicans are transcriptionally activated when galactose is present and glucose is absent in the growth medium (Brown et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2009.

claim: Most fungal species have retained the GAL1, GAL7, and GAL10 gene cluster, including several pathogenic species closely related to C. albicans such as C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis and C. parapsilosis.
source: While a few fungal species have lost the GAL1, GAL7, and GAL10 gene cluster entirely, most have retained it, including several pathogenic species closely related to C. albicans such as C. dubliniensis, C. tropicalis and C. parapsilosis (Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Hittinger et al., 2004; Slot and Rokas, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Hittinger et al., 2004; Slot and Rokas, 2010.

claim: The only known environmental niche for C. albicans is in or on warm-blooded animals.
source: Since the only known environmental niche for C. albicans is in or on warm-blooded animals (Odds, 1988), it seems very likely that the three GAL genes and their regulation is important for the ability of C. albicans to survive in its host.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Odds, 1988.

claim: The three GAL genes and their regulation is likely important for the ability of C. albicans to survive in its host.
source: Since the only known environmental niche for C. albicans is in or on warm-blooded animals (Odds, 1988), it seems very likely that the three GAL genes and their regulation is important for the ability of C. albicans to survive in its host.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the known niche of C. albicans.

claim: C. albicans GAL1, GAL7 and GAL10 genes encode enzymes necessary for galactose metabolism.
source: We experimentally verified that the closest matches to the GAL1, GAL7 and GAL10 genes in C. albicans did indeed code for the enzymes necessary for galactose metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from knockout studies.

claim: C. albicans parent strain grows normally on galactose as the sole sugar in the presence of Antimycin A.
source: We found that the C. albicans parent strain grows normally under these conditions but none of the three knockout strains could grow in the presence of Antimycin A and galactose as the sole sugar (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), a behavior similar to S. cerevisiae GAL mutants (Dudley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: C. albicans knockout strains for GAL1, GAL7, and GAL10 cannot grow in the presence of Antimycin A and galactose as the sole sugar.
source: We found that the C. albicans parent strain grows normally under these conditions but none of the three knockout strains could grow in the presence of Antimycin A and galactose as the sole sugar (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), a behavior similar to S. cerevisiae GAL mutants (Dudley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Growth of C. albicans GAL knockout strains in glucose is unaffected by the deletions.
source: Growth in glucose was unaffected by the deletions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from growth assays.

claim: The behavior of C. albicans GAL mutants is similar to S. cerevisiae GAL mutants.
source: We found that the C. albicans parent strain grows normally under these conditions but none of the three knockout strains could grow in the presence of Antimycin A and galactose as the sole sugar (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), a behavior similar to S. cerevisiae GAL mutants (Dudley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dudley et al., 2005 and experimental data.

claim: C. albicans knockout strains of GAL1, GAL7 and GAL10 all showed severe defects in a rat catheter biofilm model.
source: We found that the knockout strains of GAL1, GAL7 and GAL10 all showed severe defects (compared to a matched parent strain) in this infection model (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The defects observed for GAL knockout strains in the rat catheter biofilm model were some of the most pronounced defects observed for any previously studied gene knockout in this C. albicans biofilm model.
source: These were some of the most pronounced defects observed for any previously studied gene knockout in this C. albicans biofilm model, and the results clearly show that the GAL1, GAL7, and GAL10 genes are required for this well-characterized colonization model.
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous studies in the same model.

claim: The GAL1, GAL7, and GAL10 genes are required for the rat catheter colonization model.
source: These were some of the most pronounced defects observed for any previously studied gene knockout in this C. albicans biofilm model, and the results clearly show that the GAL1, GAL7, and GAL10 genes are required for this well-characterized colonization model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the rat catheter model.

claim: S. cerevisiae has a paralog of GAL1, called GAL3, which plays a signaling role in activating the GAL genes.
source: As a result of a whole genome 'duplication,' now known to be a hybridization between two closely related species (Marcet-Houben and Gabaldón, 2015), S. cerevisiae has a paralog of GAL1, called GAL3, which plays a signaling role in activating the GAL genes in S. cerevisiae (Bhat and Murthy, 2001; Hittinger and Carroll, 2007; Sellick and Reece, 2006, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marcet-Houben and Gabaldón, 2015; Bhat and Murthy, 2001; Hittinger and Carroll, 2007; Sellick and Reece, 2006.

claim: The whole genome duplication in S. cerevisiae is now known to be a hybridization between two closely related species.
source: As a result of a whole genome 'duplication,' now known to be a hybridization between two closely related species (Marcet-Houben and Gabaldón, 2015), S. cerevisiae has a paralog of GAL1, called GAL3, which plays a signaling role in activating the GAL genes in S. cerevisiae (Bhat and Murthy, 2001; Hittinger and Carroll, 2007; Sellick and Reece, 2006, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marcet-Houben and Gabaldón, 2015.

claim: C. albicans branched before the whole genome duplication and has only a single GAL1.
source: However, C. albicans branched before this duplication and has only a single GAL1.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic knowledge and genome analysis.

claim: C. albicans Gal1 has an activating upstream signaling role in addition to its enzymatic role.
source: Expression of the reporter was significantly lower in the presence of galactose (Figure 1C), indicating that Gal1 has an activating upstream signaling role in C. albicans, in addition to its enzymatic role.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The situation in C. albicans where Gal1 serves both enzymatic and signaling roles is similar to that in K. lactis.
source: This situation is similar to that in K. lactis, another 'pre whole-genome hybridization' species (Anders and Breunig, 2011; Hittinger and Carroll, 2007; Meyer et al., 1991; Rubio-Texeira, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anders and Breunig, 2011; Hittinger and Carroll, 2007; Meyer et al., 1991; Rubio-Texeira, 2005.

claim: The C. albicans transcriptional regulator Gal4 is clearly orthologous to S. cerevisiae Gal4.
source: The C. albicans transcriptional regulator Gal4 is clearly orthologous to S. cerevisiae Gal4, a conclusion supported by extensive phylogenetic analysis (Martchenko et al., 2007b) as well as by the fact that the Gal4 protein from both species has the same DNA-binding specificity (Askew et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Martchenko et al., 2007b and Askew et al., 2009.

claim: The Gal4 protein from both C. albicans and S. cerevisiae has the same DNA-binding specificity.
source: The C. albicans transcriptional regulator Gal4 is clearly orthologous to S. cerevisiae Gal4, a conclusion supported by extensive phylogenetic analysis (Martchenko et al., 2007b) as well as by the fact that the Gal4 protein from both species has the same DNA-binding specificity (Askew et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Askew et al., 2009.

claim: C. albicans contains a gene (orf19.6899) with ~40% amino acid identity to S. cerevisiae Gal80.
source: We note that C. albicans also contains a gene (orf19.6899) with ~40% amino acid identity to S. cerevisiae Gal80 (Wapinski et al., 2007), the regulatory protein that prevents Gal4 from activating the GAL genes in the absence of galactose (Torchia et al., 1984) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wapinski et al., 2007.

claim: S. cerevisiae Gal80 is the regulatory protein that prevents Gal4 from activating the GAL genes in the absence of galactose.
source: We note that C. albicans also contains a gene (orf19.6899) with ~40% amino acid identity to S. cerevisiae Gal80 (Wapinski et al., 2007), the regulatory protein that prevents Gal4 from activating the GAL genes in the absence of galactose (Torchia et al., 1984) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Torchia et al., 1984.

claim: The Gal80 ortholog (orf19.6899) does not play a significant role in regulating the GAL1, GAL7, and GAL10 genes in C. albicans.
source: We found that the expression of GAL1 in parent and knockout cells was similar in response to galactose and glucose (Figure 1C), demonstrating that, like Gal4, the Gal80 ortholog does not play a significant role in regulating the GAL1, GAL7, and GAL10 genes in C. albicans.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Only two knockout strains, △/△rtg1 and △/△rtg3, grew several orders of magnitude slower than the parent strain on galactose + Antimycin A.
source: We screened 212 knockout strains and found only two, △/△rtg1 and △/△rtg3, that grew several orders of magnitude slower than the parent strain under these conditions (Figure 3A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The growth defect of △/△rtg1 and △/△rtg3 strains is specific to galactose as these cells grow at normal levels on glucose, even in the presence of Antimycin A.
source: This response is specific to galactose as these cells grow at normal levels on glucose, even in the presence of Antimycin A (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Adding back the RTG1 and RTG3 genes to their respective knockout strains restores growth on galactose + Antimycin A to levels comparable to the parent strain.
source: Adding back the RTG1 and RTG3 genes to their respective knockout strains restores growth on galactose + Antimycin A to levels comparable to the parent strain (Figure 3A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Strains knocked out for CPH1 and RGT1 did not display a significant galactose-specific growth defect.
source: We note that strains knocked out for CPH1 and RGT1, transcriptional regulators previously implicated in galactose metabolism in C. albicans (Brown et al., 2009; Martchenko et al., 2007a), were represented in our library but did not display a significant galactose-specific growth defect (Figure 3A, Figure 3B—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3B—source data 1.

claim: GAL1 expression in the presence of galactose was significantly reduced in the △/△rtg1 strain and in the double mutant.
source: GAL1 expression in the presence of galactose was significantly reduced in the △/△rtg1 strain and in the double mutant (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The RTG3 deletion strain had a profound growth defect on galactose but showed no significant effect on the steady-state levels of GAL1 expression.
source: Although the RTG3 deletion strain had a profound growth defect on galactose (Figure 3A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), the deletion showed no significant effect on the steady-state levels of GAL1 expression (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 3C.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, Rtg1 and Rtg3 are basic helix-loop-helix transcriptional regulators that form a heterodimer to regulate metabolic signaling in response to mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: In S. cerevisiae, Rtg1 and Rtg3 are basic helix-loop-helix transcriptional regulators that form a heterodimer to regulate metabolic signaling in response to mitochondrial dysfunction (Jia et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jia et al., 1997.

claim: Rtg1 and Rtg3 are similar to each other in amino acid sequence, with 34% identity.
source: The two proteins are similar to each other in amino acid sequence, with 34% identity.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the protein sequences.

claim: Knockouts of RTG1 in S. cerevisiae strongly reduce metabolic signaling regulation while the RTG3 knockouts show a milder effect.
source: Knockouts of RTG1 in S. cerevisiae strongly reduce this regulation while the RTG3 knockouts show a milder effect (Hashim et al., 2014; Kemmeren et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hashim et al., 2014; Kemmeren et al., 2014.

claim: The top-scoring motif from the GAL genes in the Saccharomycotina and Kluyvermoyces clades is the Gal4 motif, with two-half sites spaced 11 nucleotides apart.
source: As expected, the top-scoring motif from the GAL genes in the Saccharomycotina and Kluyvermoyces clades was the well-documented Gal4 motif (Guarente et al., 1982), with two-half sites spaced 11 nucleotides apart (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guarente et al., 1982 and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Gal4 motif was not detected in the three GAL genes of C. albicans or any member of the CTG clade.
source: This motif was not detected in the three GAL genes of C. albicans or any member of the CTG clade.
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of genome sequences.

claim: The top motif in the GAL genes of C. albicans and CTG clade species is a longer palindromic motif, similar to the Rtg1-Rtg3 motif.
source: Instead, the top motif in these 6 species is a longer palindromic motif, similar to the Rtg1-Rtg3 motif that was identified in C. albicans (Pérez et al., 2013) and S. cerevisiae (Jia et al., 1997, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pérez et al., 2013 and Jia et al., 1997, and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Previous whole-genome ChIP experiments showed Rtg1 and Rtg3 binding peaks over the Rtg1-Rtg3 motifs in the upstream regions of all three GAL genes in C. albicans.
source: First, previous whole-genome ChIP experiments from our lab (carried out for entirely different purposes) showed Rtg1 and Rtg3 binding peaks over the Rtg1-Rtg3 motifs in the upstream regions of all three GAL genes (Pérez et al., 2013, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pérez et al., 2013 and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Rtg1-Rtg3 motif construct was induced by galactose, compared to no sugar.
source: The construct was induced by galactose, compared to no sugar (Figure 3D); this activation was absent when the motif was omitted from the construct or when RTG1 and RTG3 were deleted from the genome (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Rtg1-Rtg3 motifs, although sufficient for induction by galactose, do not completely recapitulate the behavior of the natural pGAL1 promoter.
source: We note that the Rtg1-Rtg3 motifs, although sufficient for induction by galactose, do not completely recapitulate the behavior of the natural pGAL1 promoter; in particular, the Rtg1-Rtg3 motif construct was not repressed in the presence of glucose.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of the construct behavior.

claim: Additional cis-regulatory sequences present in the natural GAL1 promoter are needed for glucose repression.
source: This observation indicates that additional cis-regulatory sequences present in the natural GAL1 promoter are needed for glucose repression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the Rtg1-Rtg3 motif alone does not confer glucose repression.

claim: Rtg1 and Rtg3 are responsible for the galactose-inducible expression of the three C. albicans GAL genes by binding directly to the cis-regulatory sequences located upstream of the genes.
source: Taken together, the results of the genetic screen, the similarity of the C. albicans GAL gene cis regulatory element to the S. cerevisiae Rtg1-Rtg3 binding site, the ChIP experiment in C. albicans, and the reporter expression experiments show that Rtg1 and Rtg3 are responsible for the galactose-inducible expression of the three C. albicans GAL genes by binding directly to the cis-regulatory sequences located upstream of the genes.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including genetic screens, motif analysis, ChIP, and reporter assays.

claim: RTG1 and RTG3 are not the only regulators of the GAL genes in C. albicans.
source: As mentioned above, we do not believe that RTG1 and RTG3 are the only regulators of the GAL genes in C. albicans.
evidence: This is based on observations that the Rtg1-Rtg3 motif alone does not fully recapitulate GAL gene regulation.

claim: The dynamic range of activation (ON vs OFF) is much larger in S. cerevisiae (~900 fold) than in C. albicans (~12 fold).
source: (1) The dynamic range of activation (ON vs OFF) is much larger in S. cerevisiae (~900 fold) than in C. albicans (~12 fold, Figure 4B–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The basal expression of GAL1 (expression in the presence of glucose and absence of galactose) is higher in C. albicans than in S. cerevisiae.
source: Two factors contribute to this difference: the basal expression of GAL1 (expression in the presence of glucose and absence of galactose) is higher in C. albicans, and the maximum expression level in C. albicans (in the presence of galactose and absence of glucose) is lower than in S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell dynamics measurements.

claim: The maximum expression level of GAL1 in C. albicans (in the presence of galactose and absence of glucose) is lower than in S. cerevisiae.
source: Two factors contribute to this difference: the basal expression of GAL1 (expression in the presence of glucose and absence of galactose) is higher in C. albicans, and the maximum expression level in C. albicans (in the presence of galactose and absence of glucose) is lower than in S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell dynamics measurements.

claim: In the absence of glucose, GAL1 begins its induction 20–40 min faster in C. albicans than in S. cerevisiae.
source: (2) In the absence of glucose, GAL1 begins its induction 20–40 min faster in C. albicans than in S. cerevisiae (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The concentration of galactose needed for half-maximal activation of GAL1 is ~15 fold lower in C. albicans than in S. cerevisiae.
source: (3) The third major difference in the C. albicans and S. cerevisiae response is the concentration of galactose needed for half-maximal activation of GAL1; it is ~15 fold lower in C. albicans than in S. cerevisiae (Figure 4C), consistent with previous observations that C. albicans is able to respond to very low concentrations of sugar (Rodaki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and consistent with a citation to Rodaki et al., 2009.

claim: In the presence of saturating concentrations of galactose, half-maximal repression by glucose occurs at lower levels in S. cerevisiae than in C. albicans.
source: (4) The opposite behavior is observed in the sensitivity of each species to glucose. In the presence of saturating concentrations of galactose, half-maximal repression by glucose occurs at lower levels in S. cerevisiae than in C. albicans (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A key property of the S. cerevisiae network is bimodal expression of pGAL1.
source: (5) A key property of the S. cerevisiae network is bimodal expression of pGAL1; that is, at intermediate levels of galactose and glucose, the population consists of mixtures of fully ON and fully OFF cells (Biggar and Crabtree, 2001; Venturelli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Biggar and Crabtree, 2001; Venturelli et al., 2015.

claim: No bimodality is evident in C. albicans across a large range of glucose and galactose ratios.
source: No bimodality is evident in C. albicans across a large range of glucose and galactose ratios (Figure 4B–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C. albicans response to galactose appears graded; at intermediate concentrations of glucose and galactose, individual cells produced intermediate levels of GFP.
source: Instead, the C. albicans response appears graded; that is, at intermediate concentrations of glucose and galactose, individual cells produced intermediate levels of GFP (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The expression dynamics of GAL1, specifically its potent induction and bimodality, is conserved across many isolates of S. cerevisiae.
source: Several groups have shown that the expression dynamics of GAL1, specifically its potent induction and bimodality, is conserved across many isolates of S. cerevisiae (Nogi, 1986; Wang et al., 2015; Warringer et al., 2011), including W303, the strain used in our analysis (Ralser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nogi, 1986; Wang et al., 2015; Warringer et al., 2011; Ralser et al., 2012.

claim: The qualitative and quantitative aspects of GAL1 induction were similar across all 12 C. albicans isolates tested, including SC5314.
source: We observed that, despite some small differences (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), the qualitative and quantitative aspects of GAL1 induction were similar across all 12 isolates, including SC5314, the lab strain used for most of our experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: None of the five differences documented between S. cerevisiae and C. albicans were observed between any two C. albicans isolates.
source: None of the five differences documented between S. cerevisiae and C. albicans were observed between any two C. albicans isolates (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The transcriptional response of S. cerevisiae and C. albicans to galactose differ in almost all of their quantitative output features.
source: We conclude from these experiments that the transcriptional response of S. cerevisiae and C. albicans to galactose—although similar in overall logic—differ in almost all of their quantitative output features.
evidence: This is based on the comprehensive comparison of quantitative features between the two species.

claim: The differences in transcriptional response to galactose are characteristic of each species as a whole and not of a particular isolate.
source: Moreover, these differences are characteristic of each species as a whole and not of a particular isolate.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of multiple isolates from each species.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, GAL1, GAL7, GAL10, and GAL2 were induced by galactose more than 275-fold.
source: In S. cerevisiae, consistent with previous work, we observed very high (>275-fold) galactose-induced expression of the three genes encoding the Leloir enzymes (GAL1, GAL7, GAL10) as well as that encoding the galactose permease GAL2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: C. albicans lacks a GAL2 ortholog.
source: In C. albicans [which lacks a GAL2 ortholog (Brown et al, 2009)], GAL1, GAL7 and GAL10 were all induced by galactose, but to a much lesser extent than in S. cerevisiae (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2009.

claim: In C. albicans, GAL1, GAL7 and GAL10 were all induced by galactose, but to a much lesser extent than in S. cerevisiae.
source: In C. albicans [which lacks a GAL2 ortholog (Brown et al, 2009)], GAL1, GAL7 and GAL10 were all induced by galactose, but to a much lesser extent than in S. cerevisiae (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The lower induction ratio of GAL genes in C. albicans is due to both higher basal expression and lower induced levels.
source: As discussed above, this lower induction ratio is due to both higher basal expression (expression in media lacking a sugar) and lower induced levels (in galactose).
evidence: This is based on RNA-sequencing data and single-cell measurements.

claim: The pGAL1 reporter is a good proxy for the GAL genes in general in both S. cerevisiae and C. albicans.
source: These observations are all consistent with the single-cell measurements described above; they also show that the pGAL1 reporter is a good proxy, in both species, for the GAL genes in general.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency between reporter data and RNA-seq data.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, 30 genes besides GAL1, GAL7, GAL10 and GAL2 are induced by galactose at least two-fold but less than 30-fold.
source: In S. cerevisiae, nearly all (28/30) genes besides GAL1, GAL7, GAL10 and GAL2 are induced by galactose, but to a much lesser extent (at least two-fold but less than 30-fold in two independent experiments, with p-values <0.01).
evidence: This is based on RNA-sequencing data analysis.

claim: Most of the 30 galactose-induced genes in S. cerevisiae are involved in some aspect of carbohydrate metabolism.
source: Most of these 30 genes are involved in some aspect of carbohydrate metabolism (Cherry et al., 2012, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on gene annotation from Cherry et al., 2012 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: In C. albicans, 33 genes met the criteria for being galactose-induced (at least two-fold induction in two independent experiments with p-values <0.01).
source: In C. albicans, 33 genes met the same criteria for being galactose-induced, yet none of them showed the higher levels of induction characteristic of S. cerevisiae GAL genes; the majority were induced between two-fold and 13-fold.
evidence: This is based on RNA-sequencing data analysis.

claim: The galactose-induced genes in C. albicans are annotated as being involved in pathogenesis, biofilm formation, filamentous growth, as well as carbohydrate metabolism.
source: These genes are annotated as being involved in pathogenesis, biofilm formation, filamentous growth, as well as carbohydrate metabolism (Inglis et al., 2012, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on gene annotation from Inglis et al., 2012 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Except for the GAL1, GAL7 and GAL10 genes, there was little overlap (only 2 additional genes, RHR2 and PFK27) between the S. cerevisiae and C. albicans galactose-induced genes.
source: Except for the GAL1, GAL7 and GAL10 genes, there was little overlap (only 2 additional genes, RHR2 and PFK27, annotated in S. cerevisiae as enzymes involved in sugar metabolism) between the S. cerevisiae and C. albicans galactose-induced genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on RNA-sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Many of the galactose-induced genes in C. albicans did not have an identifiable ortholog in S. cerevisiae and vice-versa.
source: Indeed, many of the galactose-induced genes in C. albicans did not have an identifiable ortholog in S. cerevisiae and vice-versa (Byrne and Wolfe, 2005; Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Maguire et al., 2013, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on orthology analysis supported by citations to Byrne and Wolfe, 2005; Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Maguire et al., 2013.

claim: The wiring change between S. cerevisiae and C. albicans maintained the galactose induction of GAL1, GAL7, and GAL10 but changed the remaining genes in the galactose-induced regulon.
source: These observations indicate that the wiring change between S. cerevisiae and C. albicans maintained the galactose induction of GAL1, GAL7, and GAL10 but changed the remaining genes in the galactose-induced regulon.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-sequencing data comparing the two species.

claim: The C. albicans GAL genes were observed to be induced in response to N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) in a genome-wide study.
source: Consistent with this idea, the C. albicans GAL genes were observed, in a genome-wide study, to be induced in response to N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc), a sugar derivative also known to induce genes involved in pathogenesis, biofilm formation and filamentous growth (Gunasekera et al., 2010; Kamthan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gunasekera et al., 2010; Kamthan et al., 2013.

claim: GlcNAc induced expression of the GAL genes in C. albicans, but not S. cerevisiae.
source: To further examine this observation, we measured the expression of the GAL1 promoter fusion in both C. albicans and S. cerevisiae in response to GlcNAc and observed that GlcNAc induced expression of the GAL genes in C. albicans, but not S. cerevisiae (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GlcNAc induction of GAL genes is observed in a test construct containing two Rtg1-Rtg3 binding sites driving expression of a heterologous promoter.
source: Moreover, this induction is also observed in our test construct, which contained two Rtg1-Rtg3 binding sites driving expression of a heterologous promoter (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The observed GlcNAc induction of both the artificial constructs and the natural GAL1 promoter requires Rtg1-Rtg3.
source: The observed GlcNAc induction of both the artificial constructs and the natural GAL1 promoter requires Rtg1-Rtg3 (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: The GAL genes are not required for growth on GlcNAc as a sole sugar source.
source: While the GAL genes are induced in response to GlcNAc, they are not required for growth on GlcNAc as a sole sugar source (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Y. lipolytica is an outgroup species that branched before the Candida and Saccharomycotina clades diverged.
source: To determine this, we examined Yarrowia lipolytica, an outgroup species, that is, a species that branched before the Candida and Saccharomycotina clades diverged (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic knowledge shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The Y. lipolytica genome contains clear orthologs for Gal1, Gal7 and Gal10.
source: The Y. lipolytica genome contains clear orthologs for Gal1, Gal7 and Gal10.
evidence: This is based on orthology analysis.

claim: The ability of Y. lipolytica to metabolize galactose increases when GAL genes are overexpressed.
source: Moreover, the ability of Y. lipolytica to metabolize galactose increases when these genes are overexpressed (Lazar et al., 2015), indicating that they carry out the same role as the orthologous genes in S. cerevisiae and C. albicans.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lazar et al., 2015.

claim: Y. lipolytica lacks a clear ortholog for Gal4.
source: Y. lipolytica lacks a clear ortholog for Gal4, the closest relatives being other zinc cluster proteins (Zn(II)2Cys6) lacking the surrounding amino acid sequences characteristic of the Gal4 orthologs of many other fungal species.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and orthology determination.

claim: The Y. lipolytica genome contains a single RTG ortholog (YALI0F11979) that is more similar to Rtg1 than Rtg3.
source: The Y. lipolytica genome does contain a single RTG ortholog (YALI0F11979); it is more similar to Rtg1 than Rtg3, and we will refer to the Y. lipolytica gene as RTG1.
evidence: This is based on sequence similarity analysis.

claim: In a Y. lipolytica parent strain, galactose induces GAL1 expression at least three-fold.
source: We found that in a Y. lipolytica parent strain, galactose induces GAL1 expression at least three-fold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental qPCR data.

claim: Galactose induction of GAL1 is not observed in Y. lipolytica rtg1 knockout strains.
source: This induction is not observed in two independently constructed rtg1 knockout strains (Figure 7b), indicating that this transcriptional regulator plays an important role in activating GAL1 in Y. lipolytica.
evidence: This is supported by experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Rtg1 plays an important role in activating GAL1 in Y. lipolytica.
source: This induction is not observed in two independently constructed rtg1 knockout strains (Figure 7b), indicating that this transcriptional regulator plays an important role in activating GAL1 in Y. lipolytica.
evidence: This is inferred from the knockout experiment results shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Knocking out RTG1 in Y. lipolytica did not result in a growth defect on 2% galactose.
source: We note that knocking out this regulator did not result in a growth defect of Y. lipolytica on 2% galactose (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The GAL genes in Y. lipolytica appear to be expressed at a relatively high basal level.
source: However, the GAL genes in this species appear to be expressed at a relatively high basal level.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that knockout of RTG1 does not cause a growth defect despite affecting induction.

claim: The Gal4 mode of GAL gene regulation likely arose along the S. cerevisiae lineage after S. cerevisiae and C. albicans diverged.
source: Taken together, all the phylogenetic results indicate that the Gal4 mode of GAL gene regulation likely arose along the S. cerevisiae lineage after S. cerevisiae and C. albicans diverged (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis and experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The Gal4 mode of GAL gene regulation occurred before S. cerevisiae and K. lactis diverged.
source: We also know that it occurred before S. cerevisiae and K. lactis diverged as K. lactis also uses the Gal4 mode of regulation (Rubio-Texeira, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rubio-Texeira, 2005.

claim: The tight repression of GAL1, GAL7, and GAL10 by glucose occurred much later than the Rtg1-Rtg3 to Gal4 rewiring event, specifically after S. cerevisiae branched from S. paradoxus.
source: Finally, we know from recent work (Roop et al., 2016) that the tight repression of GAL1, GAL7, and GAL10 by glucose–a defining characteristic of S. cerevisiae–occurred much later than the Rtg1-Rtg3 to Gal4 rewiring event, specifically after S. cerevisiae branched from S. paradoxus.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roop et al., 2016.

claim: The enzymes that metabolize galactose (Gal1, Gal7, Gal10) and their functions are conserved across many fungal species including S. cerevisiae, K. lactis, C. albicans and Y. lipolytica.
source: These enzymes and their functions are conserved across all kingdoms of life; direct evidence shows this is the case for many fungal species including S. cerevisiae (Dudley et al., 2005), K. lactis (Rubio-Texeira, 2005), C. albicans (Martchenko et al., 2007a, this paper) and Y. lipolytica (Lazar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dudley et al., 2005; Rubio-Texeira, 2005; Martchenko et al., 2007a; Lazar et al., 2015.

claim: A shift in the mechanism of galactose induction occurred along the evolutionary pathway to S. cerevisiae resulting in Gal4 'replacing' Rtg1-Rtg3 as an inducer of the GAL genes in response to galactose.
source: However, a shift in the mechanism of galactose induction occurred along the evolutionary pathway to S. cerevisiae resulting in Gal4 'replacing' Rtg1-Rtg3 as an inducer of the GAL genes in response to galactose.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phylogenetic and experimental evidence presented in the study.

claim: The ancestral mode of GAL gene regulation by Rtg1-Rtg3 was retained in the C. albicans clade.
source: This ancestral mode, the regulation of the GAL genes by Rtg1-Rtg3, was retained in the C. albicans clade.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phylogenetic and experimental evidence presented in the study.

claim: S. cerevisiae and C. albicans both have clear orthologs of Gal4, Rtg1, and Rtg3.
source: S. cerevisiae and C. albicans both have clear orthologs of Gal4, Rtg1, and Rtg3 (Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Wapinski et al., 2007), and these transcriptional regulators have retained their DNA-binding specificities since the two clades branched, at least 300 million years ago (Askew et al., 2009; Pérez et al., 2013; Taylor and Berbee, 2006, this paper).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Wapinski et al., 2007.

claim: The transcriptional regulators Gal4, Rtg1, and Rtg3 have retained their DNA-binding specificities since S. cerevisiae and C. albicans branched, at least 300 million years ago.
source: S. cerevisiae and C. albicans both have clear orthologs of Gal4, Rtg1, and Rtg3 (Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Wapinski et al., 2007), and these transcriptional regulators have retained their DNA-binding specificities since the two clades branched, at least 300 million years ago (Askew et al., 2009; Pérez et al., 2013; Taylor and Berbee, 2006, this paper).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Askew et al., 2009; Pérez et al., 2013; Taylor and Berbee, 2006.

claim: The rewiring of GAL genes occurred, at least in large part, through changes in the cis-regulatory sequences of the control regions of the GAL genes.
source: The rewiring therefore occurred, at least in large part, through changes in the cis-regulatory sequences of the control regions of the GAL genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of DNA-binding specificities and the observed changes in regulation.

claim: In C. albicans, the cis-regulatory sequences for Rtg1-Rtg3, located next to the GAL genes, are sufficient for galactose induction.
source: In C. albicans, we show that the cis-regulatory sequences for Rtg1-Rtg3, located next to the GAL genes, are sufficient for galactose induction; in the S. cerevisiae clade, these were 'replaced' by cis-regulatory sequences for Gal4.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from reporter assays.

claim: In the S. cerevisiae clade, the Rtg1-Rtg3 cis-regulatory sequences were 'replaced' by cis-regulatory sequences for Gal4.
source: In C. albicans, we show that the cis-regulatory sequences for Rtg1-Rtg3, located next to the GAL genes, are sufficient for galactose induction; in the S. cerevisiae clade, these were 'replaced' by cis-regulatory sequences for Gal4.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic and motif analysis.

claim: At least two differences between S. cerevisiae and C. albicans (the induction ratios of the GAL genes and the response of the GAL genes to non-galactose signals) critically depend on the rewiring.
source: Although we cannot pinpoint the extent to which the Rtg1-Rtg3 to Gal4 rewiring contributes to each of these eight differences, we can say that at least two of them (the induction ratios of the GAL genes and the response of the GAL genes to non-galactose signals) critically depend on the rewiring.
evidence: This is based on experimental evidence showing that these properties are recapitulated by Rtg1-Rtg3 binding sites.

claim: The moderate induction by galactose of the GAL genes in C. albicans is recapitulated when Rtg1-Rtg3 cis-regulatory sequences are added to a test promoter.
source: The moderate induction by galactose of the GAL genes in C. albicans is recapitulated when Rtg1-Rtg3 cis-regulatory sequences are added to a test promoter.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from reporter assays.

claim: The induction by GlcNAc in C. albicans is recapitulated in a test construct containing Rtg1-Rtg3 sites and is destroyed when RTG1 and RTG3 are deleted.
source: Likewise, the induction by GlcNAc in C. albicans is recapitulated in a test construct containing Rtg1-Rtg3 sites and is destroyed when RTG1 and RTG3 are deleted in C. albicans.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from reporter assays and knockout experiments.

claim: The features of S. cerevisiae galactose induction (high induction of GAL genes, low sensitivity to galactose concentration, high sensitivity to glucose concentration, and specificity for galactose) may be advantageous for a species that ferments different sugars rapidly.
source: Although there is no direct evidence that this rewiring was adaptive, it is tempting to speculate that the characteristics of galactose induction in S. cerevisiae—high induction of GAL genes, low sensitivity to galactose concentration, high sensitivity to glucose concentration, and specificity for galactose—are advantageous for a species that ferments different sugars rapidly (Johnston, 1999).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the adaptive significance of the observed differences.

claim: The features of C. albicans galactose induction (high basal levels and lower induction of GAL gene expression, higher sensitivity to galactose, and the inclusion of the GAL genes in a regulon that includes genes needed for pathogenesis) may be important for C. albicans to thrive in niches of warm-blooded animals where galactose is probably present at very low concentrations.
source: In contrast, the features of C. albicans (high basal levels and lower induction of GAL gene expression, higher sensitivity to galactose, and the inclusion of the GAL genes in a regulon that includes genes needed for pathogenesis) may be important for C. albicans to thrive in niches of warm-blooded animals where galactose is probably present at very low concentrations (Gibson et al., 1996).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the adaptive significance of the observed differences, supported by a citation to Gibson et al., 1996.

claim: The Rtg1-Rtg3 circuit is central to the ability of C. albicans to proliferate in a mammalian host.
source: Consistent with these ideas, we know that the Rtg1-Rtg3 circuit is central to the ability of C. albicans to proliferate in a mammalian host, as C. albicans mutants deleted for RTG1 and RTG3 are deficient in several mouse models of infection (Pérez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pérez et al., 2013.

claim: The Rtg1-Rtg3 mode of GAL gene regulation being ancestral does not mean that the ancestral fungal species resembled C. albicans in its ability to thrive in animal hosts.
source: Although we found that the Rtg1-Rtg3 mode of GAL gene regulation is ancestral, this does not mean that the ancestral fungal species resembled C. albicans in its ability to thrive in animal hosts.
evidence: This is a clarification about the interpretation of the phylogenetic findings.

claim: The Rtg1-Rtg3 circuit continued to evolve in the C. albicans clade and additional changes in this circuitry were likely needed to adapt specifically for life in a mammalian host.
source: The Rtg1-Rtg3 circuit continued to evolve in the C. albicans clade and it seems likely that additional changes in this circuitry were needed to adapt specifically for life in a mammalian host.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the evolution of the circuit in C. albicans.

claim: Transcriptional rewiring over evolutionary timescales can preserve a basic circuit output yet alter almost all of its quantitative and qualitative features.
source: This study illustrates how transcriptional rewiring over evolutionary timescales can preserve a basic circuit output yet alter almost all of its quantitative and qualitative features.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the comprehensive analysis presented in the study.
